title: The Deer Come Back at Dawn
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hook: at first light the deer return to keep their word, and the hunter lowers his bow
carry: parana: the vow ends in giving, then food
tomorrow: how do you know anything is true?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hunter's leaves and water fell on a hidden linga, and Ashutosha: Shiva is pleased by a leaf and water. Today the night ends, and so does this part of the path.
screen: `ASHUTOSHA: A LEAF IS ENOUGH.` · `THE NIGHT ENDS.`

segments.voice: The sky over the pool goes from black to gray. The hunter has been awake all night, hungry, and he has let three deer go on their word. Then he hears them. The doe, the second doe, the stag, coming back through the trees together, with their young, just as they promised. Each one steps forward and says: take me first, spare the others. Gurudruha looks at them over his bow. Something in him has changed. He lowers it, and lets them all go.
screen: `BLACK, THEN GRAY.` → `THE DEER COME BACK.` → `HE LOWERS HIS BOW.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, that's when Shiva appears. The night's worship, the leaves, the water, the waking, has worn away the hunter's hardness. Shiva gives him a new name, Guha, and a promise: one day Rama himself will come to your door. In the Ramayana, Guha is the forest chief who welcomes Rama and ferries him across the Ganga. A hunter who couldn't go home empty-handed became the man who opened his home to God. That's the shape of the morning after Shivaratri, and families still keep it. Breaking a fast at its proper time is called parana. In the Shiva Purana's account of the vow, the night doesn't end with the last song. Morning brings worship again, then giving, and only then is the fast broken. That's why many temples hand out prasad at dawn, and why a grandmother at the gate may give food away before she takes a bite. The vow closes the way the hunter's night closed: the hand that held the bow opens. It closes the Shiva part of the path, too: the pillar no one could measure, Sati and Parvati, Nataraja, a thousand names, the Shiva Sutras, the Rudram, and one great night. And here's what it asks of any big night of prayer, a fast, a festival, a vigil: the test isn't how long you lasted. It's whether the next person you meet gets fed.
screen: `THE DEER COME BACK.` · `GURUDRUHA BECOMES GUHA.` · `PARANA: WORSHIP, GIVING, THEN FOOD.` · `THE SHIVA PART, GATHERED UP.` · then, large: `THE HAND THAT HELD THE BOW OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sit as if the night has just ended and the light is coming up, and walk back slowly through its lessons: the resolve, the fast, the vigil, the name, the offering. Hold the one that stayed with you, and let it go with you into the first ordinary thing you'll do after this sit. If you pray, you can give thanks to Shiva, or to the God you know, for the night.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. The last piece: parana, the morning, when worship and giving come first and the fast is broken.
Your line: parana, the vow ends in giving, then food. The hunter lowered his bow at dawn. Same time tomorrow.
